videos.titulo: Foundations: what Sensei draws on the chart

cenas.sub: Foundations: what Sensei draws on the chart

cenas.texto: A confluence is not a certainty. It is agreement between different readings.
cenas.fala: Hello, I'm Ricardo Garcia, and this is the Sensei Bootcamp from MoreThanMoney. Before we start, I want to make one thing clear: no indicator guarantees results. Sensei brings several market readings together on one chart, with fixed rules, and shows you when those readings agree. That is different from predicting price. Over these three modules you will understand each piece of the chart, then see how a signal is born and how the trade plan is drawn, and in the last module we talk about risk, management, and a fifteen-minute daily routine. Let's go slowly. Each module builds on the one before, so don't skip ahead.

itens: Module 1 · Each piece of the chart and how to read it
Module 2 · From the score to the trade plan
Module 3 · Risk, management and daily routine
cenas.fala: The bootcamp has three modules. This first one is the foundation: what Sensei is, how you put it on your chart, and what each reading draws. The second is the engine: how a signal is born, how the score of twenty confirmations works, which filters apply, and how the plan is fixed on the signal candle, with entry, stop and four exits. The third is practice: risk per idea, position size, trade management, when not to enter, and the daily routine. I suggest you watch them in order, and pause the video whenever you want to try something on your own chart.
Let's start with the first chapter. So what exactly is Sensei?

cenas.kicker: Four lenses on the same chart
itens: Market structure
Double averages and POC
Sensei band and cloud
Order flow
cenas.fala: Sensei is built from pieces that already had a purpose of their own. The first is the structure engine from MTM Scanner, which identifies breaks and changes of character in price. The second is the double averages and the POC, which show the trend and a reference point in volume. The third is the Sensei band, an average of eighty-nine candles with one standard deviation above and below it. And the fourth is order flow, read from a lower timeframe, which tries to see who is buying and who is selling inside each candle. Picture four lenses on the same chart. Each one gives you a piece of the story. Sensei only lets an idea move forward when the lenses agree enough, and that word, agree, is the centre of the whole indicator.

itens: Double averages: trend and alignment
Volume, strength and momentum
Structure and POC
Band and buying pressure
cenas.fala: To make that agreement measurable, Sensei uses twenty confirmations, organised into four groups of five. The first group is the trend of the double averages: how they line up, their slope, and where price sits against the fast average. The second is volume, strength and momentum: volume on the signal candle, expansion in volatility, the strength of the trend measured by ADX, RSI, and order flow. The third is structure and POC: the state of market structure, changes of character, breaks of structure, the position against the POC, and the order flow imbalance. And the fourth is the band and buying pressure: the cloud, the position against the band, a recent phase, and buying pressure. Each confirmation adds one point. How many light up at the same time is the score. Later we'll see how much score you need.

itens: Forex, gold, indices and crypto
Scalp on 5 and 15 minutes
Intraday on the 1-hour chart
Swing on the 4-hour chart
cenas.fala: Sensei was designed for forex, gold, indices and crypto, and for different rhythms. In practice there are three ways to use it, and the difference is mainly the timeframe. On scalp, on the five- and fifteen-minute charts, more ideas appear and the moves are shorter, which demands more time at the screen. On intraday, on the one-hour chart, there are fewer ideas, and for many people that is a good balance, because two or three checks a day are enough. On swing, on the four-hour chart, ideas are rare and the moves tend to last longer. If you are just starting, choose one market and one timeframe for the first few weeks. Changing everything at once is the fastest way to not understand what you are looking at.

itens: A TradingView account, where the indicator runs
Sensei on your chart
A demo account with your broker
A notebook or spreadsheet for your journal
Fifteen minutes a day
cenas.fala: Before we move on, here is what you need to get the most from this bootcamp. A TradingView account, because that is where the indicator runs. Sensei on your chart. A demo account with your broker, because everything you learn should be practised without real money first. A notebook, or a spreadsheet, for your journal, which we will build in the third module. And fifteen minutes a day. What makes the difference is not how long you spend looking at charts, it is how consistently you repeat the same process over weeks.
Second chapter: how you put Sensei on your chart, and how to read the settings without getting lost.

itens: Sensei Otimizado and Estilo de Trading
Core: minimum confirmations, POC and averages
Quality filters: higher-timeframe trend, anti-sideways and candle close
Order flow, bands and structure
Risk management, breakeven and alerts
cenas.fala: When you open Sensei's settings you will see several groups, and it helps to have a mental map of them. At the top are the theme and the trading style, with the option Sensei Otimizado, which applies, for each pair and timeframe, the configuration the code has for that combination. Then the core, with the minimum number of confirmations, the POC period and the visibility of the averages. After that, the quality filters: the higher-timeframe trend, the session filter, the anti-sideways filter, and the requirement of a candle close. Further down, the buy and sell sides, the phase, the order flow with the lower timeframe, the band and the cloud. And at the end, risk management, breakeven, trailing and alerts. In this first part, the rule is simple: leave everything at the default and learn to read before you change anything.

cenas.titulo: The chart with everything switched on
cenas.fala: This is what the chart looks like with every layer switched on. At first glance it looks like a lot, and that is normal. In a few minutes you will read each element in seconds: the band around price, the averages, the POC, the structure markers, the coloured candles, the signal, the score card and the plan lines. One important note, which I will say only once in this module: the charts in this bootcamp are illustrative animations, designed to explain how things work. They are not real results and not market history. Now let's switch everything off and turn on one layer at a time.

cartoes.d: Light background. The original theme of the indicator.
A modern dark mode, for people who work at night.
Night-blue tones.
Vibrant, almost neon colours.

cenas.fala: Before we get into the readings, one practical point: the theme. In the settings, Sensei has a theme for the indicator. Light, which is the original, uses a light background. Dark is a modern dark mode. Classic uses night-blue tones. And Pop uses vibrant, almost neon colours. The logic of reading is the same in all of them, only the palette changes. Pick one and don't keep switching, because your eye gets used to the colours, and that makes reading much faster. In this bootcamp I use the original theme, so what you see on screen matches what you will find.

cenas.titulo: Reading 1: the Sensei band and cloud
cenas.sub: The eighty-nine average and its band
cenas.fala: Third chapter, and the first foundation reading: the Sensei band and the cloud.

cenas.titulo: Eighty-nine average, with one standard deviation
cenas.fala: The Sensei band is built from a simple average of eighty-nine candles, and a standard deviation, which measures how far price usually strays from that average. The upper band sits one standard deviation above the average, and the lower one a standard deviation below. Most of the time, price wanders inside that range. When it leaves it, it is moving further away than usual. Notice the colour too. The band switches between purple and grey, depending on the cloud. Purple appears when the cloud is rising, and grey when it is falling. The cloud compares a faster average with the eighty-nine average, and the colour tells you which of the two is on top. It is not a buy order. It is a reading of the direction of the background trend.

itens: Price inside the band: normal movement
Price outside the band: stretched further than usual
Purple: rising cloud
Grey: falling cloud
Position against the band is a confirmation, not a signal
cenas.fala: How do you read the band in practice? While price stays inside the range, you are in normal movement, with the market breathing around the average. When price leaves the range, above or below, it is stretched, and that deserves attention, but it is not an order. Sensei counts the position of price against the band as one of the twenty confirmations, in the band and buying pressure group. In other words, it adds one point, and nothing more. A candle outside the band, on its own, does not make an idea. In the same way, purple does not mean you should buy. It means the cloud is on the buying side. Everything depends on how the other readings behave at the same time.

cartoes.d: The original value. Changing the length changes the character of the whole band.
The original mode. The fast average in the cloud reacts faster.
The fast average is slower, and the colour changes less often.

cenas.fala: Two parameters change the character of the band. The length, which is eighty-nine by default. If you lower it, the band hugs price more closely and more moves appear outside it. If you raise it, the band becomes wider and slower. And the cloud mode: in Active, the original, the fast average reacts faster, and the colour changes sooner. In Passive, the fast average is slower, and the colour changes less often. There is no single right choice for every market. The recommendation is the same as always: change one value at a time, and observe for a few weeks before drawing conclusions.

cenas.sub: Trend and a volume reference point
cenas.fala: Fourth chapter: the double averages and the POC.

cenas.titulo: Three averages in pairs, and the POC
cenas.fala: The double averages are three exponential averages of different lengths: fifteen, fifty and two hundred and thirty-eight candles. Each has its own colour, and you read them by the order in which they line up. When the fastest average sits above the middle one, and the middle one above the slow one, the alignment is rising. When the slope of the averages also agrees, the trend is clean. Notice how the averages open out and follow each other. These alignments and slopes count as confirmations in the first group. The line of orange dots is the POC, the point of control. We explain it on the next screen. For now, keep this idea: price crossing the POC upwards is one of the buy triggers.

itens: Averages in rising order: buyer alignment
Averages in falling order: seller alignment
Averages rising or falling: strength on your side
Price above the fast average: short-term momentum
cenas.fala: How do you use the averages? Four simple ideas. First: the order. With the fastest average above the others, the alignment is for buyers. With it below, it is for sellers. Second: the slope. An average that rises gives the trend strength, and one that flattens tells you the move is losing traction. Third: the position of price against the fast average. A price above it has short-term momentum on its side. And fourth: all three together. When alignment, slope and price point the same way, the group of averages adds many confirmations. When they disagree, the score comes out lower, and that is useful information too.

itens: Calculated over blocks of fourteen candles
It is the price of the candle with the most volume in each block
Price above the POC: buyer side
Crossing the POC upwards can be a buy trigger
cenas.fala: Let's talk about the POC in plain words. Every fourteen candles, the indicator looks at the block that has just closed and finds the candle with the most volume. That candle's price becomes the POC for that block, drawn as a line of orange dots. Why does this matter? Because zones where a lot of volume traded tend to carry weight: they are references many people see. So Sensei treats price above the POC as being on the buyer side. And a crossover of price upwards through the POC is one of the two buy triggers. The other is a complete phase, which we will look at in the second module. Remember: the POC is a reference, not a guarantee that price will stop there.
Fifth chapter, third reading: market structure.

Market structure is the sequence of highs and lows that price draws. When price breaks a previous high in an uptrend, we have a break of structure, a BOS, and the trend is confirmed. When, on the other hand, price breaks an important low against the trend, a change of character appears, a CHoCH. It is the first sign that the move may have changed. The indicator also marks liquidity traps, which are moments when price pushes through a known level, catches the people who were positioned there, and then returns inside. And it draws order blocks, which are zones formed by the last candle before a strong move. All of this is context. None of these marks, on its own, is an order.

itens: BOS: structure confirms the direction
CHoCH: first hint that the move has changed
Liquidity traps: price sweeps a level and returns
Order blocks: origin zone of a strong move
cenas.fala: It is worth separating the four marks, because each one answers a different question. The BOS asks: does the trend continue? If price breaks the last high in an uptrend, the answer is yes. The CHoCH asks: is the trend still in charge? If price breaks the last important low, there is a first hint that it is not. Liquidity traps ask: who was on the wrong side? When price sweeps a known level and returns inside, many stops have been triggered. And order blocks ask: where did this move come from? The zone of the last candle before the strength can serve as a reference. These are four questions. None of them has a perfect answer, and it is the combination that gives you context.

cenas.sub: Who is buying and selling inside the candle
cenas.fala: Sixth chapter: order flow, the most technical reading in Sensei.

itens: The flow uses one-minute candles by default
Delta: buying minus selling, as a share of volume
Imbalance: when delta passes the threshold of 0.25
Without lower-timeframe data, it uses an approximation on the chart
cenas.fala: A one-hour candle looks like a box, but inside it there were many trades, buys and sells. Sensei asks the one-minute chart, which is the default timeframe for order flow, to measure how much of the volume was buying and how much was selling. The difference, divided by total volume, is called delta. When that proportion passes the threshold, which by default is zero point two five, the indicator marks an imbalance, either buying or selling. If the chart has no data from that lower timeframe, the indicator uses an approximation built from the candle itself. It is useful, but less precise. So order flow is one more vote in the score, not a reason to enter on its own.

Now it's your turn. Pause the video and read this chart on your own, layer by layer, before you continue. Where is price against the band? Is it inside or outside? What colour is the cloud? Where is price against the POC, above or below? Is there a recent BOS or CHoCH? And what do the last candles say about order flow? Answer these six questions in writing. There is no right answer for training your eye. In the next module you will see what the score says about this type of situation, and you can compare your reading with the indicator's.

cenas.titulo: Before you look at the score
itens: First the context: band and cloud
Then the direction: averages and structure
Then the flow, as a vote and not as an order
Only then look at the score
cenas.fala: Before we put everything together, a reading order that will save you a lot of time. First, the context: where price sits against the band, and what colour the cloud is. Then, the direction: the alignment and slope of the double averages, and the last structure mark. Next, order flow, which you should treat as one more vote, never as an order in itself. And only at the end do you look at the score. The reason is simple. If you start with the number, you tend to look for readings that confirm what you already wanted to do. If you start with the context, the number becomes a confirmation, and not an excuse.
Seventh chapter: let's put everything together in one example.

cenas.titulo: From the stretch to the confirmation
cenas.fala: Let's read this example calmly. Price is falling, with the cloud grey, and it reaches the lower zone of the band. Nothing has happened yet, and that is where the indicator waits. Then the structure changes character: a bullish CHoCH appears. Right after, price closes above the POC, which is the crossover that triggers a buy setup. Sensei counts the confirmations, and the signal candle closes with a score of fourteen out of twenty. That number clears the minimum of the custom style, which is twelve. The plan is drawn on the signal candle: the entry at the close, the stop one and a half ATR below, ATR being the measure of the average volatility of the candles, and the four exits above. Notice that the idea only exists after the close. Until then, it was just a reading. In the second module we will take each of these numbers apart.

itens: Buying just because price touched the band
Reading a signal before the candle closes
Ignoring the four-hour trend
Filling the chart with more indicators on top of Sensei
Changing the settings every day
cenas.fala: Before we close this module, the most common reading mistakes. First, buying just because price touched the lower band. The band is a confirmation, not a trigger. Second, reading a signal before the candle closes. Until the close, nothing is confirmed, and price can change its mind many times. Third, ignoring the four-hour trend. A buy below the two-hundred-candle average on the four-hour chart is a buy against the filter, and the filter exists for a reason. Fourth, filling the chart with more indicators on top of Sensei. It already brings together the readings you need. More lines do not give you more certainty, they give you more doubt. And fifth, changing the settings every day. That way you never get to know how the indicator behaves on your market. Choose, fix, observe.

cenas.titulo: What you need to be able to read
itens: Band: where price is against the eighty-nine average
Double averages and POC: which way the trend is leaning
Structure: whether the move keeps or changes character
Order flow: who is buying and selling inside the candle
The score only counts when the readings agree
cenas.fala: A quick recap of the first module. The band tells you where price is against the eighty-nine average. The double averages and the POC tell you which way the trend is leaning. Structure tells you whether the move keeps its character or changes it. Order flow shows who is buying and selling inside the candle. And the score only counts when these readings agree.

itens: Put Sensei on one market and one timeframe only
Turn everything off and switch on one layer at a time
Mark five times when price left the band
Note what happened next, without trading
cenas.fala: Before the second module, an exercise. Put Sensei on one market and one timeframe only, and stick with them. Turn everything off and switch on one layer at a time, as we did here. Then search the history for five moments when price left the band, above or below, and note what happened in the candles that followed. Without trading, just observing. This simple exercise trains your eye more than any video can. In the next module we will see how a signal is born, how the score is counted, and how the plan is fixed on the candle.

cenas.sub: From the score to the trade plan
cenas.texto: Educational content. Not financial advice. Trading forex, indices, metals and crypto involves high risk, and you can lose part or all of your capital. The charts in this video are illustrative. Past results do not guarantee future results.
cenas.fala: Remember: this is educational content and not financial advice. Trading carries risk, and you can lose money. Practise on a demo account first. See you in module two.

videos.titulo: From the score to the trade plan

cenas.sub: From the score to the trade plan

itens: How a signal is born
The twenty confirmations and the score
Filters that decide what reaches the screen
Trade plan: entry, stop and four exits
Alerts and reading a sell
cenas.fala: Welcome to the second module of the Sensei Bootcamp. In the first one you learned to read each piece of the chart. Now we open the engine. You will see how a setup forms, what triggers a signal, how the score of twenty confirmations works, and why the filters decide which signals reach your screen. Then we move on to the trade plan: entry at the close of the signal candle, the stop at a multiple of ATR, and the four exits in R, with the rule that the stop moves to entry after the first exit. At the end we look at alerts. This is the most technical module, so take your time, and go back whenever you need to.
First chapter: how a signal is born.

itens: Price crosses the POC upwards
Or a phase completes: Momentum or Exaustão
Only at the candle close, with the setting Apenas Fecho de Vela on
And only if the score clears the style minimum
cenas.fala: A buy setup can be born in two ways. The first is the POC crossover: price closes above a point of control that was below it. The second is a phase. Sensei counts sequences of candles, and when the count completes, the phase fires. There are two counts. One is Momentum, where the setup completes after nine candles by default, and which looks for continuation. The other is Exaustão, a countdown of thirteen candles that looks for reversals. But a setup is not yet a signal. For the signal to appear, the score must clear the minimum, the candle cannot carry order flow against the buy, and it must pass the volume and volatility filters. And with the candle-close filter on, the indicator only evaluates the candle after it has closed.

cartoes.d: Fires when the setup completes. Follows continuation. Used in the scalp and intraday styles.
Fires at the end of the full countdown. Looks for reversals. Used in the swing and conservative styles.

cenas.fala: There are two phase modes, and the choice depends on the style. Momentum is continuation: it fires when the sequence of nine candles completes, which happens when the move keeps gaining traction. Exaustão is reversal: it requires the full countdown of thirteen candles, and it looks for the point where the previous move runs out of steam. In the scalp and intraday styles, the indicator uses Momentum. In swing and conservative, it uses Exaustão. And in the optimised mode, each pair and timeframe can have its own. The rule is the same as always: don't change mode every week, because otherwise your journal cannot tell you what is working.

See how the close decides everything. While the candle is forming, price can rise and fall as much as it likes, and the indicator waits. Only after the close, with volume and volatility confirming, does the signal appear, with the score next to it. Notice that the candle that fires does not have to be the biggest on the chart. It has to be a candle that closes on the right side of the references. With the candle-close filter on, the signal never appears halfway through a candle. That matters a lot, because a signal that appears and disappears mid-candle is worthless in practice.
Second chapter: the score.

itens: Double averages aligned
Averages rising
Price above the fast average
Volume and expansion
Strength (ADX) above the minimum
RSI and order flow
Structure and change of character
Recent BOS
Price above the POC
Flow imbalance
Sensei band and cloud
Recent phase
Buying pressure
Safe volatility
cenas.fala: The score starts at zero, and every confirmation that lights up adds one. For clarity, I have arranged the twenty confirmations into fourteen pieces here, because they fit better on the screen. Each piece combines one or two readings of the same kind. Double averages aligned, and the averages rising. Price above the fast average. Volume and expansion. The strength of ADX, and RSI with order flow. Structure and the change of character. A recent BOS. Price above the POC. The flow imbalance. The band and the cloud. A recent phase. Buying pressure. And volatility in a safe zone. In this example, fourteen pieces are lit. On the indicator's panel you see all twenty, one by one, and that is where you should read. The minimum in the custom style is twelve out of twenty. Each style has its own, and the panel shows the real count.

cartoes.d: Alignment, slope, and where price sits against the fast average.
Volume, expansion, ADX, RSI and order flow.
State of structure, change of character, breaks, POC and flow imbalance.
Cloud, position against the band, recent phase, buying pressure and volatility.

cenas.fala: Twenty is a lot to memorise, so sort them into four groups of five. The first is the trend of the double averages: alignment, slope and where price sits against the fast average. The second is volume, strength and momentum: volume on the candle, volatility expansion, ADX, RSI and order flow. The third is structure and the POC: the state of the structure, the change of character, the break of structure, the POC and the flow imbalance. And the fourth is the band and buying pressure: the cloud, the position against the band, a recent phase, buying pressure and volatility. A balanced idea has pieces from several groups. A high score that comes entirely from one group deserves a more critical look, because it means one family of readings is pulling everything.

cenas.titulo: What the signal card tells you
itens: Direction: buy or sell
Score: how many pieces are lit, out of twenty
Style and phase mode in use
Whether the optimised mode was on
cenas.fala: When a signal appears, the card tells you four things, and it is worth reading them always in the same order. First, the direction: buy or sell. Second, the score, which is the number of pieces lit out of twenty. Third, the style and the phase mode in use at that moment, because the same idea can be produced by one mode or another. And fourth, whether the optimised mode was on, because that changes the configuration the indicator applied. When you write in your journal, copy these four things onto the line for that idea. Without them, a month from now you will not be able to tell why that idea was different from the others.

cenas.kicker: How to think about the score
itens: More pieces lit = more readings in agreement
It is not a probability or a promise
A high score with no structure is a warning
Always read the context above the number
cenas.fala: I want you to think about the score the right way. A high score means many different readings agree at the same time. It does not mean the idea will work. It is not a probability, and certainly not a promise. The score gives you an objective way to compare setups and decide which ones deserve your attention. A high score with no structure piece at all, for example, is a warning: the averages and volume may be saying something that price has not yet confirmed. Your job is still to read the context: the four-hour trend, the news of the day, and whether price has already moved too far from the signal.

cenas.sub: Higher-timeframe trend, anti-sideways and candle close
cenas.fala: Third chapter: the filters, which decide whether a signal with a good score actually reaches the screen.

cartoes.d: Buys only above the two-hundred-candle average on the four-hour chart. Sells only below it.
ADX blocks signals when the market has no strength. Minimum of fifteen by default.
Only evaluates after the candle has closed, so the signal does not vanish halfway.
Sells are off. When you switch them on, they require three extra confirmations.

cenas.fala: The filters are the gates a signal has to pass through. The first is the higher-timeframe trend: Sensei only lets buys through when price is above the two-hundred-candle average on the four-hour chart, and sells when it is below. This aligns the entry with the bigger current. The second is the anti-sideways filter: when ADX shows that the market has no strength, the indicator blocks signals. It is not a perfect filter, and that is why reading the market stays your job. The third is the candle close, which we have already seen. And the fourth is the side: sells are off by default, and when you switch them on the indicator requires three more confirmations than for a buy. A signal that passes all four gates is a signal with context. One that does not pass, even with a high score, should be left out.

itens: Filtro de Sessão: off, limits the hours for signals
Permitir Vendas: off by default
Só operar setups validados: off, blocks pairs with no validated configuration
Only change these three after you know the indicator
cenas.fala: There are three switches worth knowing, all off by default. The session filter, called Filtro de Sessão, limits the indicator to a window of hours that you define on the chart. Permitir Vendas, as we have seen, turns on the sell side with more demands. And the third, Só operar setups validados, blocks any pair or timeframe that has no validated configuration in the code. It is more restrictive, and it cuts exposure to combinations that have not been tested. For now, leave all three as they come. Once you have a few weeks of journal, you can try them one at a time and measure the effect in your own record.

cenas.kicker: When a signal does not come
cenas.titulo: Why a setup may not become a signal
itens: Score below the style minimum
Price on the wrong side of the four-hour 200 average
ADX below the minimum: market without strength
Setup without a candle close: not a signal yet
cenas.fala: It is worth knowing why a setup can appear and still not become a signal. There are four typical reasons. The first is the score: the crossover exists, but the number of confirmations stays below the style minimum, so there is no card. The second is the higher-timeframe trend: a buy with price below the two-hundred-candle average on the four-hour chart does not pass that filter. The third is the anti-sideways filter: with ADX below the minimum, the market does not have enough strength, and the indicator prefers to stay quiet. And the fourth is the simplest: without a candle close, there is no signal yet, only a reading in progress. When a setup does not become a signal, the indicator is not failing. It is doing the job it was designed for.

cenas.titulo: A setup that never becomes a signal
cenas.fala: Look at this illustrative chart. Price crosses the POC and the structure shows a change of character, so at first glance it seems there is an idea. But notice there is no signal card and no plan lines. In this example, the score stays below the minimum of the chosen style, because some of the pieces that usually accompany this kind of move are not lit. The indicator draws nothing, and that is exactly its job. You, on the other hand, will feel the temptation to draw the idea yourself. Don't. If the indicator did not draw it, the idea is not validated, and your journal should record it as a reading without a signal.
Fourth chapter: the styles and the optimised mode.

cenas.kicker: Choose by the time you have
itens: Scalp: 5 and 15-minute charts, more ideas, more screen time
Intraday: 1-hour chart, two or three checks a day
Swing: 4-hour chart, fewer ideas and more patience
Personalizado: you choose the minimum confirmations
cenas.fala: The styles are the first big switch. Scalp works on the five- and fifteen-minute charts, produces more ideas, and needs you at the screen regularly. Intraday works on the one-hour chart, and for someone with a job it is the most realistic: two or three checks a day are enough. Swing works on the four-hour chart, with fewer ideas, trades that last longer, and a lot of patience. And Personalizado lets you change the minimum number of confirmations, which comes at twelve, and the other parameters. Each style adjusts a whole set of things at once: the minimum confirmations, the spacing between signals, the ADX filter, the stop multiplier and the phase mode. So changing style means changing the indicator, not just the colours.

itens: Applies the code's configuration for the pair and timeframe
Replaces the chosen style whenever that configuration exists
With no configuration for that combination, it uses the chosen style
Check the settings to see which one is active
cenas.fala: Sensei Otimizado is on by default. When you are on a pair and timeframe for which the code has its own configuration, the indicator applies that configuration, and it replaces the style you picked. When there is no configuration for that combination, it falls back to your chosen style. This is practical, but it has a consequence: if you are comparing two days, it is worth checking in the settings which mode was in use, because the pair and timeframe matter more than the style. For your journal, always record the style and whether the optimised mode was on. Without that, you cannot compare one week with another.
Fifth chapter, and perhaps the most important: the trade plan.

When the idea is born, Sensei draws the full plan and fixes it on the signal candle. The entry is that candle's close. The stop sits a few ATR away, on the opposite side from the direction: by default, one and a half ATR in the custom style. The other styles and the optimised mode may use a different multiplier, so always check the value on the card. The four exits sit on the side of the direction, at multiples of the risk. That risk is called R, and it is the distance between entry and stop. The levels do not move afterwards. The dynamic levels setting is off, and that is what guarantees that the plan you see is the plan you have. Having the plan drawn before you enter is half the discipline. You know where you enter, where you are wrong, and where you take profit.

cenas.titulo: Entry, stop and exits in R
cenas.fala: Let's go through the arithmetic in words. R is the distance between entry and stop. If the stop is six points from entry, one R is six points. Exit one sits at one and a half R, which means nine points. Exit two at two and a half R, fifteen points. Exit three at four R, twenty-four points. And exit four at six R, thirty-six points. At each exit you close a quarter of the position, by default. The four percentages add up to one hundred per cent, which guarantees that if all four exits are reached, the position is fully closed. And after the first exit, the stop moves to entry. From then on, in normal market conditions, the idea no longer carries a risk of loss.

An example with round numbers, invented, on gold. Entry is at two thousand, at the close of the signal candle. The ATR of that candle is four points. The stop, at one and a half ATR, sits six points below, at one thousand, nine hundred and ninety-four. That is the R: six points. The first target, at one and a half R, is nine points above, at two thousand and nine. The second, at two and a half R, at two thousand and fifteen. The third, at four R, at two thousand and twenty-four. And the fourth, at six R, at two thousand and thirty-six. The indicator does these sums for you. But it is important that you understand where they come from, because the position size, which comes in the third module, depends precisely on this distance.

cenas.titulo: The plan does not move on its own
itens: Levels fixed on the signal candle
Dynamic levels is off by default
You are the one who moves the trade, through management
The stop only moves to entry after the first exit
cenas.fala: There are four things worth knowing about how the plan is fixed. First: the levels stay attached to the signal candle. They do not redraw when price moves. Second: the dynamic levels mode exists, but it is off. If you switch it on, the entry follows the current close and the levels recalculate on every candle. That changes the whole reading, and it is not what Sensei does by default. Third: once the plan is drawn, you are the one who moves the trade, through the management we will look at. And fourth: the only automatic change to the stop, by default, is moving it to entry after the first exit. Nothing else slides for you.

cartoes.d: By default, at Exit 1. The stop goes to entry.
Off by default. When on, the stop follows price at a distance of ATR times the multiplier, only in your favour.
Off by default. When on, reaching breakeven marks the trade as complete.

cenas.fala: There are several ways to protect a position, and they all come in a calm mode. Breakeven, by default, moves the stop to entry when Exit 1 is reached. You can choose another reference point, such as Exit 2, Exit 3, or a number of points. The trailing stop, which is off, makes the stop follow price at a distance of ATR times the multiplier. And there is also the option to treat the trade as complete once breakeven is reached, which is off too. Notice that the trailing only tightens the stop in your favour, it never moves it away. You decide whether to switch it on, and you read its effect in your journal before you keep it.

cenas.sub: The same process, in reverse, with caution
cenas.fala: Sixth chapter: the sell side. With caution, because it is switched off on purpose.

itens: Off by default
When switched on, requires three extra confirmations over a buy
Only fires below the four-hour two-hundred-candle average
The plan mirrors the buy: stop above, exits below
cenas.fala: Reading a sell is the same process, in reverse. Price stretches, the score counts, the signal candle closes on the sell side, and the plan is drawn mirrored: the stop above, the exits below. But there is an important difference. Sells are off by default, because the indicator has to be certain that the context is a sell. When you switch the sell side on, the minimum rises by three confirmations, and the trend filter only lets sells through below the four-hour two-hundred-candle average. In other words, a sell has to be a very clear sell. If you have no experience trading the sell side, leave it off and practise the reading on a demo account first.
Seventh chapter: alerts.

itens: Create an alert on the Sensei condition
Choose «any alert() function call»
Watchlist mode: one alert covers several symbols
Optional webhook, with a JSON message
cenas.fala: So you don't have to stare at the screen, you create an alert on TradingView. For the condition you pick Sensei, and then the option any alert function call. With Watchlist mode on, which is the default, that single alert sends one message for each symbol and each state of the idea. The code's frequency is once per bar, and with the candle-close filter on that respects the close of the candle. If you use a webhook, each message arrives as JSON, with the symbol, the timeframe, the style, the state, the direction, the score, the signal type and the plan levels. Notice that the score is in the message, but the context is still yours to read.

cenas.titulo: The idea followed to the end
itens: ENTRY: the idea is born, buy or sell
TP1 to TP4: each exit reached
BE: the stop should move to entry
SL: the stop has been hit
cenas.fala: After the signal, the indicator keeps following the idea, and each state has its own message. ENTRY marks the start, whether buy or sell. The TP1 to TP4 messages arrive when each exit is touched. BE tells you the stop should move to entry. And SL tells you the stop has been hit. With these message types, you can keep a journal of each idea from start to finish without having to guess what happened. That is what makes the journal honest: every idea has its entry, its exits and its end recorded.

itens: Signal = setup at the close, with the score above the minimum
The score measures agreement, not certainty
Filters decide which signals reach you
The plan is fixed: entry, stop and four exits in R
The stop moves to entry after the first exit
cenas.fala: A recap of the second module. A signal comes from a setup, at the candle close, when the score clears the minimum. The score measures agreement, not certainty. The filters decide which signals reach the screen. The plan stays fixed on the signal candle, with entry, stop and four exits in R. And after the first exit, the stop moves to entry.

itens: Go through the history of your market, on your timeframe
Find ten signals and note the score of each
For each one: style, phase mode and what happened
Count how many reached Exit 1 before hitting the stop
cenas.fala: The exercise for this module. Go through the history of your market, on your own timeframe, and find ten signals. For each one, note the score, the style and the phase mode in use. Then note what happened: did it reach the first target? Did it hit the stop? How many times did the stop have to move to entry before anything else happened? At the end, count how many reached Exit 1 before hitting the stop. That number is yours, measured by you, and it is worth more than any statistic I could give you. In the third module we take this and turn it into risk management.

cenas.fala: Remember: this is educational content and not financial advice. The numbers in this video are examples. Practise on a demo account before you risk any money. See you in module three.

cenas.texto: The score finds the opportunity. Management decides the result.
cenas.fala: Welcome to the third and final module of the Sensei Bootcamp. So far you have learned to read the chart, to understand how a signal is born and how the plan is drawn. Now comes the part that separates someone who uses a tool from someone who uses it consistently: management. The score finds the opportunity. Management decides what happens next. In this module we talk about risk per idea, position size, how to manage an idea from start to finish, when not to enter, profiles, a simple fifteen-minute daily routine, and the journal. At the end you will have a complete, written process that you can follow on a demo account starting tomorrow.

cenas.sub: The one variable you truly control
cenas.fala: First chapter: risk per idea.

cenas.titulo: Decide how much you lose before deciding how much you win
itens: You don't control the market, you control the risk
Set the risk as a percentage of the account, per idea
Many traders use between half a per cent and one per cent
Keep the same risk from idea to idea
cenas.fala: There is one thing you must accept from day one: you do not control the market. You do not control whether price reaches the first target or the stop. The only thing you truly control is how much you risk on each idea. So the first decision is not where to enter, it is how much you are willing to lose if you are wrong. That amount is set as a percentage of the account, per idea. Many traders use between half a per cent and one per cent. It is not a magic rule. It is a way to make sure that a run of losses, which will happen, does not take you out of the game. And keep the same risk from idea to idea. Someone who increases risk after a loss in order to recover is doing exactly the opposite of what they should.

Look at what happens over a run of ten losses in a row. This is not a prediction, it is arithmetic, and any method can go through a month like that. With one per cent risk per idea, after ten losses in a row you are left with about ninety per cent of the account. With two per cent, about eighty-two. With five per cent, about sixty. And with ten per cent, about thirty-five. From there, to get back to the start, you need to almost triple what is left. This is just maths, and it is the reason small risk is not cowardice, it is survival. The numbers are examples, and they have no relationship to the indicator's performance.
Second chapter: position size.

itens: Cash risk: account times percentage
R: the distance from entry to stop, which Sensei shows
Value per unit: what one pip or one point is worth per lot
The lot comes from the numbers, not from intuition
cenas.fala: Position size is worked out with a simple formula. First, the cash risk: the value of the account times the percentage you have decided to risk. Second, R, the distance between entry and stop, which Sensei already shows you on the plan, in pips for forex and in points for indices, gold and crypto. Third, the value per unit: what one pip or one point is worth per lot, on your instrument and with your broker. The size is the cash risk divided by R times the value per unit. The important consequence is this: the lot changes from idea to idea. When the stop is close, the lot is bigger. When it is far, the lot is smaller. What stays the same is the cash risk.

An example with round numbers, on a forex pair. The account is ten thousand. You decide to risk one per cent, which is one hundred. Sensei shows the stop is twenty pips from entry. On a pair where one pip is worth ten per standard lot, the calculation is one hundred divided by twenty times ten, which gives half a lot. If the stop were forty pips away, the lot would be a quarter. The cash risk always stays at one hundred. Always confirm the pip value on your platform, because it changes with the pair and with the account currency. And if the calculated lot is smaller than your broker's minimum, the idea simply does not fit your account. Let it pass.

cenas.titulo: When the minimum lot does not fit
itens: The broker's minimum lot sets the smallest possible risk
A far stop on a small account can exceed your limit
In that case, the idea is not for that account
Alternatives: a lower timeframe, another instrument, or waiting
cenas.fala: A situation that comes up often with small accounts. The broker has a minimum lot, normally one hundredth of a lot. That minimum sets the smallest risk you can have on an idea. If the account is small and the stop is far away, even the minimum lot can risk more than your limit. When that happens, the honest answer is: this idea is not for your account. You do not increase the risk to make it fit. The alternatives are to trade a lower timeframe, where stops tend to be shorter, to choose an instrument with a smaller value per point, or simply to wait for the next idea that fits. Letting pass an idea that does not fit is risk management working.
Third chapter: how to manage an idea from start to finish.

itens: Higher-timeframe trend in your favour: buy above the 4-hour 200 average
Market with strength: the anti-sideways filter helps, but you confirm too
Candle closed: the signal came at the close
Score above the minimum and no empty groups
Size calculated from the risk
cenas.fala: Before you enter, do a thirty-second check. Is the four-hour trend in your favour? Buys above the two-hundred-candle average, sells below it. Does the market have strength? The anti-sideways filter helps, but you confirm it too, with the chart. Is the candle closed, and did the signal come at the close? Is the score above the minimum of your style, and are there whole groups empty? And is the lot calculated from the stop, and does it fit your risk? If any answer is no, you let it pass. Other ideas will come. An idea you never entered has never cost you money.

cenas.titulo: You enter at the close, with the plan written
cenas.fala: Entry is taken at the close of the signal candle, with the size calculated from the risk. In this indicator, the plan is drawn on the signal candle, and the entry is that close. See how the card shows the score of fourteen out of twenty, and how the plan lines are already on the chart before anything has happened. Nothing else is needed to decide. If the idea does not meet what the check asked for, then you do not enter, even if the card looks attractive. The plan is only useful if it is followed with the same discipline on the good ideas and on the bad ones.

During the idea, management has three moments. Until the first target, your only task is to watch the stop and the structure. At Exit 1, you close a quarter of the position and move the stop to entry. From then on, the idea should no longer cost you money, in normal market conditions. Then, at each following exit, you close another quarter, until you have no position left at Exit 4. In the meantime, there are three reasons to exit before the last target, and they are written in the strategy guide. If the structure changes character against you. If the cloud stops being purple and turns grey. Or if the score drops. You do not exit because you are nervous. You exit because the reason for the entry no longer exists. And what you must not do is move the stop further away. Never.

And when the idea fails? Look at this example. The idea appears, price rises a little, but does not reach the first target. Then it falls back, and hits the stop, which sits one and a half ATR from entry. The loss is one R, plus broker costs, and it was planned before you entered. There is no surprise, no improvising, and no reason to move the stop halfway. Losing one R is the plan working. What must not happen is losing two, three or ten R on one idea, because you moved the stop. Over many ideas, what separates those who last from those who do not is exactly this discipline. Losing a little, and in a planned way, is part of the process.
Fourth chapter: when not to enter. A large part of the discipline is letting ideas pass.

itens: Against the four-hour 200-candle average
Sideways market, without strength
Score on the limit, with whole groups empty
Price already far from entry
A sell taken without knowing it is switched off, and without the extra confirmations
cenas.fala: There are five situations in which you should let the idea pass. First: the four-hour trend is against it. A buy below the two-hundred-candle average is a buy against the bigger current, and the filter exists for that reason. Second: the market is sideways, without strength. The anti-sideways filter helps, but you also have to look. Third: the score is right at the minimum and whole groups are empty. Fourth: price is already far from entry. If you arrived late, you arrived late, and chasing price ruins the relationship between risk and exits. And fifth: a sell taken without knowing that sells are switched off, and without the extra confirmations they require.

itens: Central bank decisions and employment or inflation data
An economic calendar shows the times
At those moments, price can jump through your levels
Decide in advance what you will do with an open idea
cenas.fala: There is one thing the indicator cannot see: the calendar. Central bank interest-rate decisions, employment data and inflation data can move the market violently within seconds. In those moments, price can jump over your stop, and the technical reading loses its meaning for a few minutes. The practical rule, which is a choice you make, is not to open ideas in the minutes before and after these events. If you have an idea open, decide before the news what you will do: protect it, close part of it, or leave. An economic calendar is easy to check, and it fits well into your daily routine.
Fifth chapter: choosing your profile.

cenas.titulo: Pick one and stick with it

cartoes.d: 5 and 15 minutes. Many ideas, needs screen time and quick decisions.
1 hour. Two or three checks a day are usually enough.
4 hours. Few ideas, longer trades, a lot of patience.

cenas.fala: There are three typical profiles. Scalp, on the five- and fifteen-minute charts. It gives more ideas, but it demands screen time and quick decisions, which makes it the most demanding. Intraday, on the one-hour chart, is the one I recommend for people with a job: two or three checks a day are usually enough. And swing, on the four-hour chart, with few ideas and trades that last longer. It demands patience above all, because you can go days with nothing to do. Pick a profile and stick with it for at least a few weeks before you change. Every change of profile is a change of method, and your journal needs time to show you what works.

itens: Week 1: only read, don't trade, and note the signals
Week 2: trade on demo, with a fixed risk per idea
Week 3: demo with full management and a journal every day
Week 4: review the journal and decide the next steps
cenas.fala: To make this concrete, here is a four-week plan. In the first week, you only read. You open your market on your timeframe, and note each signal that appears and what happened next. In the second week, you trade on a demo account, with a fixed risk per idea, without worrying about perfect management. In the third week, still on demo, you apply full management: the plan, protection at Exit 1, the four exits, and you write in the journal every day. In the fourth week, you review everything. How many ideas came up? In how many did you follow the plan? What was the average result in R? Only after that do you decide the next steps. Four weeks sounds like a long time, but it is the shortest route to not losing money while you learn.
Sixth chapter: the fifteen-minute daily routine.

itens: Check today's economic calendar
Open your market on your timeframe
Check the four-hour trend and the position against the 200 average
Review the signals received and the open ideas
Update the journal
cenas.fala: The routine fits into fifteen minutes. First, today's economic calendar, so you know at what times there are high-impact events. Second, you open your market on your timeframe, always the same one. Third, you check the four-hour trend and the position of price against the two-hundred-candle average: is the bigger current in favour of buys or sells? Fourth, you review the signals you received and the ideas you have open, and you apply the management we have seen. Fifth, you update the journal. For the rest of the day, the alerts work for you. You don't need to be glued to the screen. You need to be consistent.

itens: How many signals appeared and how many you traded
In how many you followed the plan
Average result in R
Where your mistakes were
One single change for next week
cenas.fala: On top of the daily routine, set aside half an hour a week for the review. Count how many signals appeared and how many you traded. In how many you followed the plan. What the average result in R was. And where your mistakes were: did you enter late, move the stop, ignore an exit, skip the check? Then decide on one single change for the following week. Only one. If you change five things at once, you will not know which one made the difference. The weekly review is the moment you stop reacting to the market and start improving your process.

cenas.titulo: Write it down, even when it went well
itens: Date, market, timeframe and direction
Score, style and phase mode
Result in R, not in money
Did you follow the plan? Yes or no
One sentence: what you learned
cenas.fala: After each idea, whether it went well or badly, you write in the journal. Date, market, timeframe and direction. The score, the style and the phase mode in use. The result measured in R, not in money, because R can be compared across ideas, accounts and lot sizes. The most important question: did you follow the plan, yes or no? And one sentence about what you learned. After thirty or forty ideas, the journal tells you things no video can tell you: on which market and at which hours Sensei works best for you, and where you, not the indicator, are falling short.

linhas: Waited for the candle close, did not enter halfway
cenas.fala: Here is what one line of the journal looks like, in an invented example. The fifth of November, gold, one-hour chart, buy. Score fourteen out of twenty, with the intraday style. Entry at the close of the signal candle. On management: a quarter closed at Exit 1, at one and a half R, and the stop moved to entry. The rest of the position came out at entry, with no loss. A quarter at one and a half R gives zero point three seven five R, so the result comes out at roughly plus zero point four R. Did you follow the plan? Yes. And the learning: I waited for the close and did not enter halfway. Notice there are no cash values. R lets you compare ideas over months. And the learning can be about something that went well. The journal is not only for mistakes.
Seventh chapter: the trader's mind. Some mistakes no indicator can fix.

itens: Revenge: raising risk to recover a loss
Fear of missing out: entering late, far from the signal
Overconfidence: skipping the check after winning
Moving the stop further away
cenas.fala: There are four classic mistakes, and almost everyone goes through them. The first is revenge: you lose an idea and raise the risk on the next one to get it back. It is the fastest way to turn a bad day into a bad week. The second is fear of missing out: you see an idea running well, you enter late, far from the signal, and your stop ends up in the wrong place. The third is overconfidence: after three or four good ideas in a row, you skip the thirty-second check because you think you no longer need it. And the fourth, the most dangerous, is moving the stop further away when price gets close to it. If you recognise yourself in any of these, don't feel bad. Write it in the journal. Seeing the pattern written down is the first step to breaking it.

cenas.titulo: Limits set with a cool head
itens: A maximum number of losses per day
Once reached, you close the platform
A mandatory pause after a large loss
A weekly journal review, always on the same day
cenas.fala: The best way to protect yourself from these mistakes is to set rules with a cool head, before you open the chart. For example: a maximum number of losses per day, after which you close the platform, whatever happens. A mandatory pause after a loss bigger than usual. And a weekly journal review, always on the same day, in which you look at the numbers in R and at the answer to the question: did you follow the plan? These rules seem simple, and they are. The difficult part is keeping them on the days the market tests you. That is why you write them down before.
Eighth chapter: the questions that come up again and again.

itens: Does Sensei repaint? With Apenas Fecho de Vela on, the signal is only evaluated at the close
Can I switch sells on? Yes, but three extra confirmations are required
Should I change the parameters? Only after weeks of journal, and one at a time
Do I need several timeframes? Read a higher one for the trend, and trade just one
cenas.fala: First question: does Sensei repaint? With the Apenas Fecho de Vela filter on, the signal is only evaluated after the candle closes, not halfway through it. Second: can I switch sells on? You can, but know that the sell side requires three extra confirmations, and that the trend filter only lets sells through below the four-hour two-hundred-candle average. Third: should I change the parameters? Only after a few weeks of journal, and always one at a time, so you know the effect of each change. Fourth: do I need several timeframes? You can look at a higher timeframe to read the trend, but trade just one, so you don't contradict yourself.

itens: What if several fail in a row? Check whether you followed the plan
Raising the minimum confirmations gives fewer signals
Can I trade only the strongest signals? You can, but there will be fewer
How long until real money? The journal tells you
cenas.fala: A few more questions. What if several ideas fail in a row? It is normal, it happens with any method. The right question is not whether the indicator has stopped working, it is whether you followed the plan in each of them. Raising the minimum number of confirmations gives fewer signals, and that is your choice, which has to be tested in the journal. Can I trade only the strongest signals? You can, but there will be few, and you need patience to wait weeks for one. And finally: how long until I am ready for real money? There is no number. Your journal tells you. When you follow the plan consistently for several weeks, with fixed risk, you are treating this as a process. That is the goal.

itens: Expectancy = the average of the R won and lost per idea
It is measured in your journal, after many ideas
Positive: the process has an edge in your hands
Negative: review your execution before blaming the indicator
cenas.fala: One last idea that ties everything together. After thirty, forty or fifty ideas, you can calculate your expectancy: the average of the R won and lost per idea. You add up all the results in R and divide by the number of ideas. If that number is positive, the process, in your hands, has an edge. If it is negative, before you blame the indicator, review the execution: did you follow the plan? Did you respect the stop? Did you enter late? Very often the difference lies there. This number is yours, measured by you, on your market. No video, no guru and no indicator can give you that number. Only your journal can.

itens: Higher-timeframe trend in your favour
Market with strength
Candle closed
Score above the minimum
No empty group
Size by risk
Stop at entry at Exit 1
Journal written
cenas.fala: To close, the Sensei pocket checklist. Higher-timeframe trend in your favour. Market with strength. Candle closed. Score above the minimum, and no empty group. Size calculated from the risk. Stop at entry at Exit 1. And the journal written. Eight steps. If you follow them every time, even when it is tedious, you are already ahead of most people who try to trade without a method.

cenas.texto: More than indicators: method, time and discipline.
cenas.fala: We have reached the end of the Sensei Bootcamp. Thank you for getting through all three modules. Remember what I said at the beginning: Sensei does not decide for you, it brings readings together and shows you when they agree. The rest is process, patience and controlled risk. Do the exercises, practise on demo, write your journal, and bring your questions to the community. I'm Ricardo Garcia, and this is MoreThanMoney.
